description: We are a student team interested in space, games, coding, and technology. We want to build a fun and educational game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. We are looking for teammates interested in coding, game development, design, 3D art, space science, data, and storytelling. If you love space and want to create something together, join us!
summary:
RoverOps is a free browser game that turns students into a Mars rover mission team. Players choose a mission, design a rover from 19 parts, program it with visual code blocks, then press RUN and watch their plan succeed or fail on real Mars terrain. Every part changes mass, power, speed, grip and cost, and every mission has a mass limit, so players face the same trade-offs real mission engineers do: there is no perfect rover, only good decisions. When a mission fails, the game explains why, and players redesign and try again.

All 14 missions take place at real landing sites, and some recreate real events from NASA's Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity rovers. The terrain is built with MarsForge, our open-source tool. MarsForge turns NASA MOLA, HiRISE, CTX and THEMIS data and ESA HRSC elevation into playable 3D Mars, with real rocks found by our own AI model.
RoverOps makes space mission design something students can try, fail and learn from, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does
RoverOps lets students run a Mars rover mission from start to finish. Each mission follows the loop real rover teams use:

  1. Pick a mission: read the objective and three star goals, such as “analyse the target rock” or “send a photo to the lander”.
  2. Design the rover: choose wheels, camera, battery, solar panel and drill from 19 parts. Each part changes mass, speed, grip, power use and cost. The rover can’t launch over the mission’s mass limit.
  3. Plan the mission: program the rover with visual code blocks (movement, If/Else, loops, sensor readings and science actions). As with a real rover controlled from Earth, there is no joystick.
  4. Run and learn: watch the plan play out in 3D. If it fails, the game explains why (wheels slipping on a steep slope, battery empty, wrong rock analysed), and the player fixes the design and runs it again.

How it answers the challenge
The challenge asks for a game where players design and manage a mission while trading off limited resources. RoverOps does this for the surface operations phase of a mission:

  • Mass: heavier rovers accelerate more slowly and use more energy.
  • Power: driving, drilling and the camera drain the battery, and solar panels recharge it. A dust storm halves speed and doubles power use.
  • Budget: Space Points earned from stars buy better parts.
  • Data and communications: limited memory, and the rover must reach the lander to send data back to Earth.
  • Terrain and time: grip limits the slopes the rover can climb, and star goals reward efficient missions.

There is rarely one right answer. A light, fast rover and a heavy, strong rover can both succeed, and players discover this by testing.

Real Mars, real history
All 14 missions take place at real landing sites, from Curiosity’s Gale Crater to the Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity sites. Later missions recreate real events: Sojourner analysing the rock Barnacle Bill, Spirit surviving dust storms and driving backwards on a broken wheel, and Opportunity finding the “blueberries” and escaping Eagle Crater.

MarsForge: turning NASA data into playable Mars
We built MarsForge, an open-source tool, to make the terrain. Draw a box on the NASA Mars Trek map, and MarsForge:

  • builds 3D terrain from the NASA MOLA + ESA HRSC elevation model,
  • finds real rocks in NASA HiRISE images with RockBoxNet, our AI model,
  • predicts rocks and soft soil where there are no HiRISE images, using a model we trained on NASA CTX images, THEMIS night-time heat data and elevation,
  • exports everything as FBX for the game.

Benefits and impact
Students usually only read about mission trade-offs. RoverOps lets them make the decisions, fail safely and try again. It teaches engineering (mass, power, traction), coding (sequences, conditions, loops, sensors, debugging) and Mars science, starting from zero knowledge. It runs in any web browser with nothing to install, so any student with a link can play, including students in places like Rajshahi, Bangladesh, where we live.

What makes it creative

  • Failure is the teacher: every crash explains itself.
  • Real NASA data and real mission history, not an invented planet.
  • Our own AI pipeline turns orbital data into rocks and soft ground the rover must deal with.
  • An in-game AI Assistant builds a working program for stuck players, but it costs Space Points, so players still have to think.

Tools and languages

  • Game: Unity 6 (URP), C#, built for WebGL.
  • MarsForge: C#/.NET, WPF, Helix Toolkit, GDAL, ONNX Runtime.
  • AI models: Python (training), ONNX (deployment).

Factors we considered

  • Making it easy for beginners
  • Keeping trade-offs realistic but simple
  • Browser performance
  • Honest use of data: where HiRISE images don’t exist, rocks are predicted, not real

What we’d build next

  • Team mode for up to 4 players with roles (rover engineer, mission planner, science lead, communications)
  • Launch and landing-site planning
  • A mission editor for teachers using MarsForge
  • End-of-mission reports

Use of SI: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code, writing, and video editing.
